cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf assamica, notably the Jinggu Dabai bud type
processing: Large-leaf shoots are withered slowly indoors, out of direct sun, for two to three days until the leaf top darkens and the downy underside stays white, then dried at low temperature; a little more oxidation than Fujian white tea. Sold loose or pressed into cakes and dragon balls.
harvest_season: Spring, from March to April, for the best lots; autumn tea is also made and is cheaper.
appearance_dry: Big two-tone shoots, black-brown on top and silvery white underneath, with fat downy buds.
appearance_wet: Large, soft olive-brown leaves with pale fuzzy buds.
taste_profile: Fruity and honeyed with apricot, grape and a floral lift, a thick sweet body and a faint bitterness in the finish; bolder and juicier than Fujian whites.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at 90–95 °C. Large leaf and buds take a while to open; keep the first steeps short because assamica leaf can turn bitter. Good cold-brewed.

vintage_note: Sold both as the current year's spring (or autumn) tea and aged, loose or pressed into cakes and dragon balls with the year stated; 2–5 years is common and it ages toward honey and dried apricot. It is cheaper than Fujian white tea of equivalent grade. Some sellers file it under black or sheng rather than white because of its higher oxidation; the wither-only process makes it a white tea.
description:
Yue Guang Bai, 'moonlight white', is Yunnan's white tea: the province's big-leaf assamica shoots, withered and dried instead of being made into pu-erh, with the result that each leaf is dark on top and white underneath, 'like moonlight on a dark night'. The story that it is withered by moonlight is best taken as a legend, and when the name first appeared is poorly documented; the tea is real and good. It comes mainly from Jinggu and the Simao hills in Pu'er prefecture, and from Lincang.

It is withered indoors, out of direct sun, for two or three days, longer and a little warmer than Fujian white tea, so the leaf oxidises more at the surface while the downy buds stay silver, and then it is dried gently. The Jinggu Dabai bush, a large-bud type, gives the fat buds that make the best lots; bud-only versions are sold as Yunnan Silver Needle.

In the cup it is juicier and bolder than anything from Fujian: apricot and grape, honey, a floral lift, a thick sweet body and a faint assamica bitterness at the end that keeps it from being cloying. Brew it at 90–95 °C with short early steeps, since the big leaf can turn bitter, and it runs seven infusions; it is also one of the best teas for cold brewing. Aged a few years it goes deeper into honey and dried fruit.

It is sold as the current year's spring tea, as cheaper autumn tea, and aged, loose or pressed into cakes and dragon balls with the year on the label. Its category is argued about, since it oxidises more than Fujian white and some sellers call it a black or even a sheng; by process, wither and dry only, it is a white tea. The practical warning runs the other way: fat Yunnan buds are often sold as Fujian Silver Needle. A dark underside and a heavier, fruitier cup give them away.

Try it next to a Fuding Mudan and a young sheng from the same Yunnan hills: it sits exactly between them.
sources_note: No dedicated English Wikipedia article found. The 2000s origin of the 'moonlight' name follows market history; some producers claim older roots.
history:
Moonlight White comes from Yunnan, with Jinggu the place most often named, and it is made from the province's large-leaf bushes. When it first appeared is poorly documented.

The name has two stories. One holds that the leaf is dried by moonlight rather than sun, which is best taken as a legend. The other points to how it looks: dark on top, pale and downy underneath, with bright buds.

Its place in the tea families is still argued. It is made along white-tea lines but is sometimes filed under pu-erh or even black tea.
